en.title: The Book of De · Chapter Thirty-four · The Use of Arms
en.原文:
用兵有言曰吾不敢為主而為客
吾不進寸而芮尺

是胃行无行
襄无臂
執无兵
乃无敵矣

𠪾莫於於无適无適斤亡吾吾葆矣

故稱兵相若
則哀者勝矣
en.字龕:
### 兵 *bīng* — arms

**字 Graph** ｜ 篆 ![兵之篆](/book-assets/hosuke-laozi-en/zhuan/%E5%85%B5.svg)

**文 Gloss** ｜ The *Shuowen*: 「兵，械也。從廾持斤，并力之皃。」 — "A weapon. From 廾, two hands, holding 斤, the axe: the look of joined force."

**像 Image** ｜ Two hands lifting an axe. The graph holds no enemy — only the weapon, and the hands that must answer for it.

**義 Sense** ｜ The whole chapter turns on what those hands do *not* do: not strike first, not advance the inch. Arms are instruments of ill omen; the graph keeps the adze in plain sight so that reluctance has something to look at.

（校勘附記 · collation note）The silk text (MS A) writes 芮 where MS B and Wang Bi have 退, "retreat": 芮 is young grass newly sprung — tender and close to the ground. The retreat reading comes from collation with 退, not from the graph itself.
en.對校:
用兵有言﹕「吾不敢為主而為客，不敢進寸而退尺。」是謂行無行，
:
攘無臂，扔無敵，
:
執無兵。
禍莫大於輕敵，輕敵幾喪吾寶。
:
故抗兵相加，哀者勝矣。

en.校記:
This chapter follows Manuscript A (MS A) throughout. Graphs are those outside the brackets in the *Changsha Mawangdui Han mu jianbo jicheng* (2014; hereafter *Jicheng*). The original editors remark that MS A's text of this chapter is full of scribal errors; the graphs are recorded as they stand and corrected in the notes below.

- 用兵有言曰吾不敢為主而為客: Follows MS A; Manuscript B (MS B) writes 又 for 有, read as 有. Wang Bi reads 用兵有言：吾不敢為主而為客.
- 吾不進寸而芮尺: Follows MS A. The original editors note that for MS A's 吾不 all other texts have 不敢; MS B and the Peking University manuscript read 不敢進寸而退尺, as do the received texts. MS A writes 芮 where MS B and Wang Bi have 退 "to fall back". (*Jicheng* IV, p. 35, n. 168)
- 是胃行无行 / 襄无臂 / 執无兵: Follows MS A; MS B writes 攘 "to bare the arm", and MS A's 襄 is read as 攘. In MS A, 執 was struck through in red. Wang Bi has an extra line, 扔無敵, after 攘無臂 and before 執無兵. (*Jicheng* IV, p. 35, n. 170)
- 乃无敵矣: Follows MS A; MS B lacks 矣. The *Jicheng* points out that 矣 is absent from all other texts, including MS B and the Peking University manuscript; by adding it MS A seems to take 乃 in its ordinary sense ("then") rather than as 扔, though this sits awkwardly with the next line, 禍莫大於无敵. Wang Bi lacks this line and instead has 扔無敵 above. (*Jicheng* IV, p. 35, n. 169)
- 𠪾莫於於无適无適斤亡吾吾葆矣: Follows MS A, which writes 𠪾莫於於无﹦適﹦斤亡吾吾葆矣, with repetition marks after 无適. The original editors note that 大於 is miswritten 於於 (the first 於 struck through in red but not corrected) and that 吾葆 has a superfluous 吾. 𠪾 is 禍 "calamity" — on the plate 厤 above 心, though the *Jicheng* prints a form with 咼 and 㤅; 適 is read as 敵 "match, enemy", 斤 as 近 "near to", 葆 as 寶 "treasure". MS B reads 禍莫大於無﹦敵﹦近亡吾𤥯矣; at its 亡 a graph was first spoiled and then circled for deletion, printed 〇 in the *Jicheng*. (*Jicheng* IV, p. 35, n. 170; p. 203, n. 136)
- 无適: MS A has 无適, MS B 無敵, as does the Peking University manuscript; most received texts have 輕敵 "taking the enemy lightly", Fu Yi alone 無敵, and Gao Ming holds that 無敵 is original and 輕敵 a later alteration. Wang Bi reads 禍莫大於輕敵，輕敵幾喪吾寶. (*Jicheng* IV, p. 35, n. 169)
- 故稱兵相若: Follows MS A; MS B, the Peking University manuscript and the received texts all have 抗 for 稱 (the Peking University manuscript writing 亢). MS A's 若 is struck through in red; the original editors gloss 若 as "to match" and suspect that the received 加 is a miswriting of 如; MS B, the Peking University manuscript, Fu Yi and several Dunhuang manuscripts all read 相若. Wang Bi reads 故抗兵相加. (*Jicheng* IV, p. 35, n. 171)
- 則哀者勝矣: Follows MS A; MS B reads 而依者朕□, with 依 read as 哀 "grieving" and 朕 as 勝, its last graph lost. Wang Bi reads 哀者勝矣, without 則.
en.疏:
杳眇曰：用兵之道，老子言之審矣。「不敢為主而為客」，為主者先發制人，是尚強也；為客者後人而動，待敵而應，是貴柔也。先發者以意奪人而失應變，應敵者隨敵而動故無不中。此與世俗兵家先發制人之說截然相反，老子以不先為勝，斯其要也。「不敢進寸而芮尺」，帛書作「芮」，王弼作「退」。芮有縮義，比退更為內斂。不進寸而退尺者，進一步之欲不如退一尺之不傷，此柔中之至者也。

「行无行，攘无臂，執无兵」，文義一貫。行而似不行，揚臂而似無臂，執兵而似無兵——似無而實有，敵見其形不見其實，欲攻而無著力處。此隱形之兵，无敵云者，非无敌人也，乃无形可窺、无迹可尋，敵自不敢犯之謂也。帛書以「乃无敵矣」收束排句，王弼本改作「扔無敵」而移置排中，收束之力遂失。

至甲本「𠪾莫於於无適」（𠪾即禍字；無「大」字而「於」字重出，疑抄手之誤），乙本作「禍莫大於無敵」，與王弼本「輕敵」異，此二本差異最大而人多忽之。適者，匹也、配也。无適，謂天下莫與為配，無可匹敵之謂也。何以无適反為禍？無敵則驕，驕則輕，輕則失慎，失慎則反受其害。「无適斤亡吾葆」（甲本；斤讀為近，葆讀為寶）——亡慈、亡儉、亡不敢先之三寶皆自无適生。輕敵是果，無敵是因；王弼止言其果，帛書直探其因，此帛書義深於王弼者也。前章「三寶」以慈為寶，慈故能勇，慈心既亡，勇無由生，故曰近亡。

「故稱兵相若，則哀者勝矣」。哀者非懼非弱，乃心存惻怛、不輕用死者。兵力相當之時，懷惻隱者用兵必慎而得宜，血氣好闘者雖強必敗。此慈故能勇之兵法落實也。哀者，不輕敵也。嗟乎！兵者不祥之器，聖人不得已而用之，恬淡為上，不以其美。知无適之為禍，則知三寶之可寶；知哀者之能勝，則知慈柔之為本——治身治世，一以貫之者也。
en.疏英:
Yaomiao says: on the use of arms, Laozi has spoken with care. "I dare not play the host, but play the guest": to play the host is to strike first and force the issue — exalting strength; to play the guest is to move after the other, answering the enemy as he comes — prizing the soft. He who strikes first seizes by intent and loses the power to answer; he who answers moves with the enemy and so never misses. This stands flat against the military men's doctrine of preemptive strike: Laozi wins by never going first — that is the crux. "Dare not advance an inch, but fall back a foot": the silk text writes 芮, Wang Bi writes 退. 芮 carries shrinking inward — more gathered-in than retreat. Not gaining an inch but yielding a foot: the desire for an inch's advance is not worth a foot's retreat from harm — the utmost of the soft within.

"Marching with no march, baring no arm, wielding no weapon" — one thread of sense. Marching yet seeming not to march; an arm raised yet seeming armless; a weapon held yet seeming weaponless — seemingly absent, really present. The enemy sees the shape but not the substance; he would strike and finds no purchase. This is the invisible army. "No enemy" does not mean no enemy exists — it means no form to spy out, no track to follow, so the enemy dares not offend. The silk text closes the series with the four words 乃无敵矣, "and so, no enemy"; the Wang Bi recension recasts them as 扔無敵 and folds them into the middle of the series — the closing force is lost.

Then "no calamity is greater than having no match" — manuscript A writes 𠪾莫於於无適 (𠪾 is 禍, "calamity"; A lacks 大 and writes 於 twice, likely a copyist's slip), manuscript B 禍莫大於無敵 — against Wang Bi's 輕敵, "taking the enemy lightly." Here the two texts diverge most widely, and most readers miss it. 適 is a match, a peer. Having no match means none in all-under-heaven can stand against you. Why should that be calamity? **Unmatched, one grows proud; proud, one grows careless; careless, one loses vigilance; vigilance lost, one suffers the very harm.** "Having no match comes close to losing my treasures" (A: 无適斤亡吾葆, 斤 read as 近, 葆 as 寶) — the loss of nurturing love, of thrift, of not daring to stand first: the three treasures die of having no match. Lightness toward the enemy is the fruit; having no match is the root. Wang Bi names the fruit; the silk text goes straight to the root — here it runs deeper. Among the three treasures of the previous chapter, nurturing love is the first: nurturing love makes one brave; the nurturing heart dead, bravery has nowhere to grow — hence "close to losing."

"So when armies are raised and evenly matched, it is the sorrowing side that wins." The sorrowing one is neither fearful nor weak: his heart holds the aching fellow-feeling, and he does not spend death lightly. When strength is equal, the side that pities uses arms with care and measure; the side hot for blood, however strong, must lose. This is "nurturing, one can be brave," enacted in the art of war. The sorrowing one is he who does not take the enemy lightly. Ah — arms are instruments of ill omen; the sage uses them only when he must, prizing calm detachment, finding no glory in them. Know having-no-match for the calamity it is, and you know the three treasures for treasures; know the sorrowing side for the winner, and you know nurturing softness for the root — governing the self and governing the world, one thread through all.
en.英譯:
The masters of arms have a saying: I dare not play the host, but play the guest; I do not advance an inch, but fall back (芮) a foot.

This is called: march, yet seem not to march; raise an arm, yet seem armless; hold a weapon, yet seem weaponless — and so, no enemy.

No calamity is greater than having no match (无適). Having no match comes close to losing my treasures.

So when armies are raised and evenly matched — it is the sorrowing side that wins.

校記:
本章帛書原文全據甲本；字從《集成》（2014）括號外原字。原注謂甲本此章誤字太多，今照錄原字，出校於下。

- 用兵有言曰吾不敢為主而為客：從甲本；乙本「有」作「又」，讀為「有」。王弼本作「用兵有言：吾不敢為主而為客」。
- 吾不進寸而芮尺：從甲本。原注謂「吾不」各本作「不敢」，乙本、北大本皆作「不敢進寸而退尺」，傳本同。甲本「退」作「芮」，乙本、王弼本作「退」。（《集成》肆·頁35·注168）
- 是胃行无行　襄无臂　執无兵：從甲本；乙本「襄」作「攘」，「襄」讀為「攘」。甲本「執」字原以硃塗過。王弼本「攘無臂」下有「扔無敵」一句，次於「執無兵」之前。（《集成》肆·頁35·注170）
- 乃无敵矣：從甲本；乙本無「矣」字。《集成》謂「矣」字各本（包括乙本、北大本）所無，甲本加之，似不讀「乃」為「扔」而用其常義，然如此則與下句「禍莫大於无敵」相牴。王弼本無此句，而於上文作「扔無敵」。（《集成》肆·頁35·注169）
- 𠪾莫於於无適无適斤亡吾吾葆矣：從甲本。甲本作「𠪾莫於於无﹦適﹦斤亡吾吾葆矣」，「无適」下有重文號；原注謂「大於」誤作「於於」（上一「於」字用硃塗過而未改），「吾葆」衍一「吾」字。「𠪾」即「禍」，圖版上厤下心，《集成》印作从咼从㤅之形；「適」讀為「敵」，「斤」讀為「近」，「葆」讀為「寶」。乙本作「禍莫大於無﹦敵﹦近亡吾𤥯矣」，其「亡」字處原有一字寫壞，圈去作廢，《集成》以〇代之。（《集成》肆·頁35·注170；頁203·注136）
- 无適：甲作「无適」，乙作「無敵」，北大本同；傳本大都作「輕敵」，唯傅奕本作「無敵」，高明以為本應作「無敵」，「輕敵」乃後人所改。王弼本作「禍莫大於輕敵，輕敵幾喪吾寶」。（《集成》肆·頁35·注169）
- 故稱兵相若：從甲本；乙本、北大本及傳本「稱」皆作「抗」（北大本寫作「亢」）。甲本「若」字用硃塗過，原注謂若訓當，通行本作「加」，「加」疑「如」字之誤；乙本、北大本、傅奕本及數種敦煌寫本皆作「相若」。王弼本作「故抗兵相加」。（《集成》肆·頁35·注171）
- 則哀者勝矣：從甲本；乙本作「而依者朕□」，「依」讀為「哀」，「朕」讀為「勝」，末字殘。王弼本作「哀者勝矣」，無「則」字。
